title: Persuasive & Argumentative Writing
description: Crafting compelling arguments — structure, rhetorical appeals, counter-arguments, tone, evidence, and calls to action.

notes.heading: Argument Structure
notes.body: Persuasive writing follows a clear structure: (1) Hook — grab attention (startling fact, question, anecdote). (2) Context — establish why this issue matters. (3) Thesis — your position clearly stated. (4) Body paragraphs — each developing one reason with evidence. (5) Counter-argument — acknowledge opposing view, then refute. (6) Call to action — what you want the reader to DO. Strongest arguments typically go last (build to your best point). Weaker arguments in the middle. Address emotional and logical appeals — pure logic is dry; pure emotion is manipulative. The most persuasive writing blends both.

illustration.alt: Flow diagram of the six steps of a persuasive argument: hook, context, thesis, body paragraphs, counter-argument, and call to action.
illustration.caption: A persuasive argument flows through six stages, from the opening hook to the closing call to action.

notes.heading: Ethos, Pathos, Logos in Depth
notes.body: Aristotle's three appeals: Ethos (credibility/character) — establish why readers should trust you. Demonstrate expertise, acknowledge complexity, use credible sources, maintain fair tone. Pathos (emotion) — connect with readers' feelings. Use vivid examples, personal stories (anecdotes), emotionally resonant language. But don't manipulate — emotion should serve truth. Logos (logic/reason) — build rational case. Use facts, statistics, logical reasoning, cause-effect relationships. Address: 'If X, then Y. Evidence shows X is true. Therefore, we should...' The strongest persuasion uses all three: 'As a doctor with 20 years' experience (ethos), I've watched families devastated by this disease (pathos). The data shows a 73% reduction when early screening is implemented (logos).'

notes.heading: Counter-Arguments and Rebuttal
notes.body: Addressing opposing views strengthens your argument dramatically. It shows you've considered other perspectives and still find your position stronger. Structure: (1) Acknowledge fairly — don't straw-man. (2) Refute with evidence/reasoning. (3) Explain why your position is still stronger. Example: 'Some argue that school uniforms suppress individuality (acknowledgement). However, research consistently shows that uniforms reduce socioeconomic visible inequality, decrease bullying, and allow students to focus on learning rather than fashion competition (rebuttal with evidence). The evidence suggests that temporary suppression of clothing choice is outweighed by long-term educational benefits.' Placement: typically before your strongest point or just before conclusion.

notes.heading: Persuasive Language Techniques
notes.body: Rhetorical question: engages reader, implies answer. 'How many more must suffer before we act?' Inclusive language: 'we,' 'us,' 'our' — builds solidarity. Direct address: 'you' — makes reader feel personally addressed. Repetition/anaphora: repeating key phrases. Tricolon: three parallel elements. Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for impact. Emotive language: words carrying strong emotional associations. Modality: high modality (must, will, certainly, undoubtedly) conveys confidence. Low modality (might, could, perhaps) suggests uncertainty — use strategically. Imperatives/commands: 'Act now.' 'Don't wait.' Expert opinion: quoting authority boosts ethos. Statistics/data: '73% of...' Anecdote: short personal story making abstract issues concrete.

notes.heading: Opening and Closing with Impact
notes.body: Openings: start with a question, shocking statistic, vivid image, anecdote, or bold statement. Avoid: 'In this essay I will...' Hook readers immediately. The opening sets tone and creates curiosity. Closings: end with impact. Restate position in fresh language. Synthesise arguments — don't just list them. End with: call to action (what now?), warning of consequences, vision of a better future, powerful quotation, or return to the opening image (circular structure). The final sentence should resonate. Never end weakly with 'That's all I have to say.' Your conclusion is your last chance to persuade — make it count.

notes.heading: Logical Fallacies to Avoid
notes.body: Weak arguments rely on fallacies: Ad hominem — attacking person, not argument. Straw man — misrepresenting opponent's position. False dichotomy — only two options when more exist. Slippery slope — one step leads inevitably to catastrophe. Bandwagon — 'everyone believes it.' Appeal to authority without genuine expertise. Hasty generalisation — broad conclusion from thin evidence. Red herring — distracting with irrelevant point. Circular reasoning — conclusion restates premise. To strengthen YOUR argument: check for fallacies in your own writing, anticipate fallacies opponents might use and be ready to expose them.

notes.heading: Adapting to Audience and Purpose
notes.body: Effective persuasion adapts to audience. Consider: Who are they? What do they already believe? What do they value? What objections might they have? Formal audience (academic, professional): emphasise logos and ethos, measured tone, sophisticated vocabulary. General public: blend pathos and logos, accessible language, relatable examples. Hostile audience: acknowledge their concerns, find common ground, build bridges before arguing. Supportive audience: reinforce shared values, inspire action, stronger pathos. Purpose: are you trying to change minds? Inspire action? Reinforce existing beliefs? Each requires different emphasis. MYP assessment values awareness of audience and purpose.

flashcards.definition: Appeal to credibility/character — establishing why the audience should trust you.
flashcards.example: 'As a marine biologist who has studied coral reefs for 30 years...'

flashcards.definition: Appeal to emotion — connecting with audience's feelings, values, and imagination.
flashcards.example: 'Imagine watching your child's future disappear, day by day, as the forests burn.'

flashcards.definition: Appeal to logic/reason — using facts, statistics, evidence, and rational argument.
flashcards.example: 'Carbon emissions have risen 47% since 1990, correlating directly with a 1.2°C temperature increase.'

flashcards.definition: Acknowledging opposing views then refuting them with evidence — strengthens credibility.
flashcards.example: 'Some may argue... However, this overlooks the evidence showing...'

flashcards.definition: A clear statement of what you want the audience to DO after being persuaded.
flashcards.example: 'Sign the petition today. Write to your MP. Make your voice heard before it's too late.'

flashcards.definition: Question asked for persuasive effect, not expecting an answer. Engages the audience.
flashcards.example: 'If not now, when? If not us, who will stand up for the voiceless?'

flashcards.definition: Degree of certainty expressed. High: 'must,' 'will,' 'certainly.' Low: 'might,' 'could,' 'perhaps.'
flashcards.example: High modality conveys confidence. Low modality shows uncertainty — use carefully.

flashcards.definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack.
flashcards.example: 'You want to reduce military spending? So you want to leave our country defenceless!' (distortion).

flashcards.definition: Using 'we,' 'us,' 'our' to build solidarity and shared purpose with audience.
flashcards.example: 'We all want a better future for our children. Together, we can make it happen.'

flashcards.definition: A short personal story making an abstract issue concrete and emotionally resonant.
flashcards.example: 'Last year, I met a farmer whose entire crop was destroyed by drought — not a statistic, but a person.'

flashcards.definition: Words chosen for their emotional impact rather than just their literal meaning.
flashcards.example: 'Innocent children' vs 'young people.' 'Devastating consequences' vs 'significant effects.'

flashcards.definition: Ending by returning to the opening image/idea — creates satisfying closure.
flashcards.example: Open with image of a burning forest. Conclude by revisiting that image — now showing regrowth.
